name: Nora Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five and at the Halvorsen farm by six, out on Mill Road past the old dairy. First job is checking the ewes and the twenty-odd beef cattle, then feeding, then whatever Arne tells me, fencing or hauling straw or sorting potatoes in the shed. I only started three years ago, after the Brookvale dairy plant shut and I lost my packing job, so I'm still the one who gets told how to do things.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the animals and I like being outside, even in the rain, which surprised me. What wears me out is my knees and my back, and the money, honestly. It's the lowest pay on the farm, Per's school bus wage covers the rest, and we've never got more than a few weeks ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let it stay hype. At the farm we'd just carry on, Arne would grumble about the price of feed like always, and nobody would talk about computers. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something saying the money should go to hospitals instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change my worries one bit. I'm on the bottom wage, we've got less than a month put by, and old Mr Halvorsen keeps saying his son might sell the sheep. AI being a flop doesn't fix any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up at six and try to learn the lambing properly this spring, so I'm worth keeping. We'd keep the car another few years and skip the holiday to see Ingrid in the city. I'd also keep pushing Per to ask about the bus drivers' union rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Not scared of robots in this one, just worn down by the same old sums at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the son might sell the sheep. What would that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half my work is the sheep, so I'd be down to part-time potatoes and cattle. I don't think they'd keep me full hours, I'm the newest and the slowest. I'd have to find something else around here, and there isn't much, maybe the care home or the petrol station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you cut first if hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone and the television package go first, they're easy. After that it's the car, and that's the hard one, because the farm is eight miles out and there's no bus at six in the morning. Without the car I can't get to work at all.

say: I'd say I'm **glad** it's hype and the money should go to **hospitals** instead.
At the farm we'd **carry on** as normal, with Arne grumbling about **feed prices**.
think: The flop doesn't touch my real worry: the **lowest wage** and under a month saved.
The owner's son might **sell the sheep**, which is half of my work.
do: Learn **lambing** properly this spring so the farm sees me as worth keeping.
Keep the old car and **skip the trip** to see Ingrid in the city.
Push Per to ask about the bus drivers' **union rate**.
feel: **Tired** and worn down by the same **money sums**, though not afraid of robots.
S0.quote: I'm on the bottom wage, we've got less than a month put by, and old Mr Halvorsen keeps saying his son might sell the sheep.
fieldNote: Her worry is **already there** before AI: low pay, thin savings and a farm that may shrink.
She sees the **car** as the line she can't cross, because the farm is eight miles out.
Her progressive views show in small ways, such as wanting money for **hospitals** and union pay for Per.

steps.text: Learn lambing properly with Arne this spring
Skip this year's trip to see Ingrid in the city
Drop the phone and television package if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say watch out, because the office jobs go first and then they come for the rest of us. At the farm I'd tell Arne to keep an eye on the Halvorsens' accountant, because if a computer does the books, the next thing it does is decide who's needed. Online I'd share the union posts about protecting workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me directly, not much at first. I don't plan anything or write anything, I carry feed and fix fences. But Ingrid's hospital admin friends and Mats's parts counter at the garage, that's where I'd worry, and when the young ones lose work they come looking for farm jobs like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the farmworkers' union, which I've been meaning to do for two years. It's about twelve a month, and I'd find it somewhere. I'd keep my head down and keep working, and I wouldn't touch any of these AI programs, I don't trust them with anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the kids, and a bit cornered for myself. I'm not the one it hits first, but I'm the one with nothing to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said young people would come looking for farm jobs. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a lad, Tobias, who used to work the feed merchant's order desk in town. If a computer takes his orders, he's twenty-five and strong. A lad who loses his order desk job in town would get hired over a 58-year-old woman with bad knees in a heartbeat. I don't even blame Tobias for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies selling this stuff, and the government for letting them do it with no rules. Nobody asked us. If they're going to make billions off it, some of that should come back to people like us as training or a decent pension.

say: I'd warn that **office jobs** go first and the rest of us **come next**.
I'd share **union posts** about protecting workers online and tell Arne to watch the **accountant**.
think: My own work is carrying feed and fixing fences, so it **won't hit me first**.
Young people who lose **desk jobs** will want farm work, and they'd **beat me** to it.
do: Join the **farmworkers' union** at about twelve a month, after two years of meaning to.
Keep working and **avoid AI programs** completely, because I don't trust them.
feel: **Uneasy** for my children and a bit **cornered** about myself.
S1.quote: A lad who loses his order desk job in town would get hired over a 58-year-old woman with bad knees in a heartbeat.
fieldNote: She understands her hands-on work is **safe for now**, but sees **competition** coming from younger people pushed out of desk work.
She blames **big companies** and a government that set no rules, not the young workers.
Joining the union is her one **concrete step**, and she frames it as long overdue.

steps.text: Join the farmworkers' union and pay the monthly fee
Keep doing the feeding and fencing without any AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws and a proper safety net, and I'd say it loud. At the farm I'd ask Mr Halvorsen straight out what he's planning, and online I'd sign every petition going. People like me need to hear that someone has a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the robots in 2031 that frighten me. I'd be 63, still four years off my pension, and if a robot can lamb a ewe and fork straw, the newest hand on the farm is the first one out. The thinking part doesn't matter to me, I don't do any, but the Halvorsens' planning and ordering would all go to a computer straight away, and I think that's the first step to machines in the shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd join the union and go to the meetings, not just pay. I'd cut everything we don't need, the car insurance down to the basic, no more takeaway on Fridays, and try to put fifty a week aside before 2031. And I'd ask Ingrid whether there's room for us near her if it all goes, which I'd hate to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, picturing it. Like standing on a road with something coming and nowhere to step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Per that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we've got three years to stop living week to week, and we've never once managed that in thirty years. Then I'd probably make tea and not sleep. Per would say something will turn up, he always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate to ask Ingrid. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because she's a nurse on night shifts with two little ones, and she's got enough on. A mother is supposed to help her daughter, not land on her doorstep at 63. But if the government won't help, family is all there is.

say: I'd demand **laws** and a proper **safety net**, and say it loudly.
I'd ask Mr Halvorsen **straight out** what he plans and sign every **petition**.
think: Robots arriving in **2031** would hit me at 63, **four years** before my pension.
Computers taking the farm's **planning and ordering** first feels like the start of **machines** in the shed.
do: Go to **union meetings** in person, not just pay the fee.
Cut car insurance to basic and stop Friday takeaways to save **fifty a week**.
Ask Ingrid whether there's **room nearby** if the farm job goes.
feel: **Sick** with dread, like standing on a road with **nowhere to step**.
S2.quote: If a robot can lamb a ewe and fork straw, the newest hand on the farm is the first one out.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** before robots matters to her only as a countdown, because she's the **newest hand**.
Her public anger at the government covers a private fear of **leaning on her daughter**.
She's never saved for thirty years, so **fifty a week** is a big ask she isn't sure she can keep.

steps.text: Go to farmworkers' union meetings in person every month
Sign petitions for laws protecting farm workers from robots
Cut the car insurance to basic and stop Friday takeaways
Ask Ingrid about moving near her if the farm job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: this needs rules and it needs them now, while there's time. I'd say it at the union meeting and to anyone at the shop on Mill Road who'd listen. Five years is long enough for the government to get something in place, if it bothers to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2034 means I'd be 66, so I'd be holding on for the last year before the pension. That's still a year with no wage on less than a month saved. But it's not the nightmare of the fast one, it's more like an awful last stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union this winter and push for a deal where the oldest workers keep their jobs until pension age. I'd try to put twenty-five a week into the credit union, which is about what I can do without the car going. I'd keep doing lambing and cattle and not learn any computer stuff, I'm too old to start fiddling with tablets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and stubborn, I suppose. Like I'd dig my heels in and try to last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd dig in. What if Mr Halvorsen asked you to learn the new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight that I'm not the right person, and he should ask Arne or a young one. I'd rather muck out by hand than stand there with a tablet getting it wrong. That probably makes me easier to let go, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the twenty-five a week cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The meal at the pub on my birthday, the bird seed, little things like that. Per likes his football subscription, and I'd have a hard time asking him to drop it. Five years of that adds up, though, maybe six thousand, which would carry us through that last year.

say: I'd say this needs **rules now**, while there's still **time** to make them.
I'd raise it at the **union meeting** and in the shop on Mill Road.
think: Robots in **2034** hit at 66, leaving one year **without a wage** before the pension.
It's an **awful last stretch** rather than the nightmare of the fast picture.
do: Join the union this winter and push for **pension-age protection** for older workers.
Put **twenty-five a week** into the credit union, aiming for about six thousand.
Stay on lambing and cattle and **refuse tablet work** on new machines.
feel: **Uneasy** and **stubborn**, ready to dig in and last.
S3.quote: I'd rather muck out by hand than stand there with a tablet getting it wrong.
fieldNote: The extra years turn panic into a **savings target**: about six thousand to cover the last year.
Her refusal to learn the machines is honest, and she knows it **makes her easier** to let go.
She wants a **union deal** protecting older workers until pension age, which is her real ask.

steps.text: Push the union for older workers to keep jobs until pension age
Put twenty-five a week into the credit union for five years
Keep lambing and feeding cattle by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so there's no excuse for leaving workers behind. I'd still talk it up at the union. But I'd also say to people my age, this one isn't really about us, it's about our kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039 means I'd be 71, so the farm job runs out on its own before the machines come. That's a relief, I won't pretend otherwise. What still worries me is the same old thing: the low wage and a pension that won't stretch, and the farm might still sell the sheep long before any robot shows up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mostly keep going as I am and work until 67. I'd put a bit by when I can, and I'd vote for whoever promises a decent state pension and rules on this stuff. I'd tell Mats to get something with his hands that a robot can't easily do, maybe heating engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer for me, worried for Mats and Ingrid. Strange to feel relieved that I'm old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mats exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him, you've got ten years, don't waste them at that parts counter waiting for a computer to take it. Go do the heating course at the college while you're thirty. I'd tell my son Mats to do the heating course while he's thirty, not fifty-five like me. He'd roll his eyes, but he'd hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money worry stays. How much does it weigh compared to the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More, honestly, in this one. The robots are far off, but the gas bill is next month. I'm still the one at the kitchen table with the calculator.

say: Ten years leaves **no excuse** for leaving workers behind.
This picture is mostly **about our kids**, not people my age.
think: Robots in **2039** come after I'm 71, so the job ends **on its own** first.
The old worries stay: a **low wage**, a thin **pension** and maybe losing the sheep.
do: Keep working at the Halvorsen farm **until 67** and save a bit when possible.
Vote for a decent **state pension** and rules on AI.
Tell Mats to do the **heating course** while he's thirty.
feel: **Relieved** for myself but **worried** for Mats and Ingrid.
S4.quote: I'd tell my son Mats to do the heating course while he's thirty, not fifty-five like me.
fieldNote: With a decade, the robot threat passes her by, but her mood stays low because of **money worries**.
Her advice shifts to **her son**, urging him to train while young.
She weighs the **gas bill** next month above robots ten years off.

steps.text: Keep working at the Halvorsen farm until 67
Vote for parties promising a decent state pension
Urge Mats to start the heating course at the college

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, the fast one, because the robots would get to the farm while I'm 63 and the newest hand. What would help is a guarantee that older farm workers keep a wage or a bridge payment until pension age, and a union strong enough to make it stick.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who does the work nobody wants. It's people like me, late starters on the bottom wage. Nobody plans for late starters on the bottom wage when anything changes, robots or not.

headlineQuote: Nobody plans for late starters on the bottom wage when anything changes, robots or not.
portrait: Nora is 58 and has worked as the **newest hand** on a sheep, cattle and potato farm since the dairy plant closed.
She lives on the **lowest wage** with her partner Per, a school bus driver, and less than a month saved.
She never uses **AI tools** and refuses to learn tablets, though she knows that makes her easier to replace.
She blames **big companies** and the government, and wants a union and rules to protect older workers.
Fast robots **alarm** her most, while ten years leaves her relieved but still worried about **money**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would reach the farm at 63, four years before her pension.
whatWouldHelp: A **bridge payment** or job guarantee for older farm workers until **pension age**.
A **strong union** able to make that guarantee stick.
